claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloys maintain greater structural stability at high temperatures than conventional mono- or bi-metallic nanoalloys.
High-entropy nanoalloys maintain greater chemical stability at high temperatures than conventional mono- or bi-metallic nanoalloys.
A multi-component alloy composition induces local lattice distortions.
Persistent chemical disorder suppresses the initiation of phase segregation and grain growth.
The as-synthesized high-entropy nanoalloys are nanocrystalline and have a uniform multi-element distribution.
Inert or reducing atmospheres minimize oxidation during high-temperature treatment.
Configurational entropy stabilizes the crystal lattice of a multi-principal-element nanoalloy.
Configurational-entropy stabilization operates by introducing lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions hinder atomic mobility.
Local lattice distortions hinder particle or grain coalescence.
Reduced atomic mobility and coalescence reduce phase segregation and grain growth at high temperature.
After identical high-temperature exposure, high-entropy nanoalloys will undergo less phase transformation than conventional nanoalloys.
After identical high-temperature exposure, high-entropy nanoalloys will exhibit less grain growth than conventional nanoalloys.
After identical high-temperature exposure, high-entropy nanoalloys will retain a more uniform elemental distribution than conventional nanoalloys.
Conventional nanoalloys will exhibit more oxidation than high-entropy nanoalloys under similar high-temperature conditions.
The predicted stabilization applies only below the composition-dependent miscibility or phase-instability threshold.
Above the miscibility or phase-instability threshold, thermal degradation or surface oxidation may dominate the material response.
